chunks: There is no god but Allah! O Prophet of Allah, I am the first to believe in you and to acknowledge that the tree did what it did just now with the command of Allah, the Sublime, in testimony to your Prophethood and to heighten your word.
Upon this all the people shouted, 'Rather a sorcerer, a liar; it is wonderful sorcery, he is very adept in it. Only a man like this (pointing to me) can stand testimony to you in your affairs.'
ai.seo_question: What did the narrator say to confirm the Prophet's prophethood through the tree's movement?
ai.summary: In this passage from *Nahj al-Balagha*, the narrator (often identified as Ali ibn Abi Talib or a close companion depending on the specific narration variant) asserts his primacy in faith by linking the miraculous movement of the tree directly to divine will as confirmation of Muhammad’s prophethood. The crowd’s dismissal of him as a 'sorcerer' highlights the early Meccan/Medinan dynamic where physical miracles were often met with skepticism or attributed to magic rather than divine truth, a theme central to Shia reflections on the nature of *Iman* and *Kufr*. This incident underscores the concept of *Tasdiq* (verification) through signs, reinforcing the Shia emphasis on the Prophet’s authority being validated by clear, observable miracles (*Mu'jizat*).

en.sayed-ali-raza: There is no god but Allāh! O Prophet of Allāh, I am the first to believe in you and to acknowledge that the tree did what it did just now with the command of Allāh, the Sublime, in testimony to your Prophethood and to heighten your word”.
Upon this all the people shouted, “Rather a sorcerer, a liar; it is wonderful sorcery, he is very adept in it. Only a man like this (pointing to me) can stand testimony to you in your affairs.”
